effect_mechanism: The units that set the class point toward a biodiversity loss, but none states how large it is. A review of nature-based solutions states that if non-native tree plantations replace intact native ecosystems such as ancient grasslands, peatlands or woodlands, the outcomes for biodiversity will be poor [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1]. On the Orissa coast of India, extensive Casuarina plantations established as a storm protection measure caused destruction to olive ridley sea turtle nesting beaches [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12]. The same review reports research in north-west India showing that although afforestation activities can lead to an aggregate increase in forest cover, in most cases they result in loss of diversity and promote monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4]. Against this, the review allows a gain in a narrower case: establishing plantations of non-native trees in a highly degraded landscape might benefit biodiversity locally if the trees enable native vegetation to regenerate, or regionally if plantations take pressure off native biodiverse forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. An INRAE expert synthesis's own small meta-analysis of species richness in plantations against natural regeneration of the stand after regeneration cutting finds no clear difference: -0.24, a very imprecise estimate from a very small number of cases, with an interval that spans zero [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1].
conditionality: The loss is stated without a size: the loss-side units are review statements and a cited case, none of which quantifies the decline against the land a plantation replaced, so the row reports a direction only and its strength is not quantified. What separates loss from gain is what the plantation replaces: intact native ecosystems, a nesting beach or a diverse cover replaced by monocultures on the loss side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4], a highly degraded landscape where the trees help native vegetation return on the gain side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. The only quantified comparison against regeneration is non-significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1]. Further INRAE statements point toward loss — plantations generally lead to decreases in biodiversity, or at least to changes in composition at the expense of native species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_6], and a cited 40% loss of local species richness in forest plantations relative to uncut control forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_2] — but they are held out of the class because their comparator is reference forest, not the starting point of a restoration project, so they describe a shortfall from a natural baseline rather than a restoration effect. The INRAE evidence is temperate and boreal, and only the Indian cases come from the low- and lower-middle-income target; the north-west India finding was re-homed to this family from active planting because it describes monoculture afforestation. The plantation family is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up, because plantation monocultures may not count as a nature-based solution, and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline.

effect_mechanism: A global review finds planted forests and woodlots have the highest CO2 removal rates, 4.5 to 40.7 t CO2/ha/yr during the first 20 years of growth [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_1], and plantation reforestation with cyclical harvest accumulates a modelled median of 44.6 tC/ha across aboveground and belowground biomass, soil and harvested wood products [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_2]. Soil carbon also rises: afforestation of cropland raised soil organic carbon stocks by 26% on average and tropical transitions to plantation gained 0.919% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_2], and the compiler for afforestation of degraded irrigated cropland in Uzbekistan reports surface biomass growth of 20 t/hectare/year and soil organic matter up by 20% in the form of fallen leaves [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1533_2011_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1533_2011_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C].
conditionality: Soil gains are conditional: on pastures (3%) and natural grasslands the change was not significantly different from zero, boreal sites lost 1.5% while other zones gained 7 to 17%, low-clay soils showed no change, heavily disturbed site preparation cut the gain to 4% against 19% with low disturbance, and plantation density made no difference [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_10]; that meta-analysis draws mostly on high-income temperate sites. The planted-forest removal range spans eucalyptus, teak and pine among other species, and the modelled 44.6 tC/ha counts harvested wood products and is a discounted present value [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_2]. These are production-plantation results, planted forests, woodlots and plantations under cyclical harvest. Whether the plantation family belongs in the forest-restoration roll-up at all is an open decision for the team, so read this row as plantation evidence, not as restoration toward a natural baseline.

effect_mechanism: This row asks how much water leaves the catchment after forest cover is restored or expanded, and the evidence finds both less and more, with close to even weight on each side. Measured syntheses mostly find less: in about 80% of study cases reporting annual water yields the effect of forest restoration and other forms of forest cover expansion was negative, and in 6% positive [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1]; baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]; groundwater levels or recharge decreased with forest cover expansion in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; and no study in the meta-analysis subset showed a water-yield gain [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The reason given is interception and use: tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, and much of the water that soaks in is used by the trees [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed, and that planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]; after clearance, the streamflow gain declines as new cover establishes, and a return to pre-cut totals under natural regrowth may take more than eight years [ev_water_yield_ham08_8]. Planting shows the same: a cited New Zealand study notes afforestation reducing water yield while giving erosion benefits [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4]; a global review warns that large-scale afforestation in water-limited environments will inevitably exacerbate water scarcity [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. On the gain side, baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]; a regional land-climate model projects significant increases of 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% in four regions under full reforestation potential [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]; about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed showed increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% for a 12.6% increase in forest cover [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]; and forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3].
conditionality: What separates the sides is baseline, method, species and time. The losses come from measured syntheses that pool forest restoration with other forms of forest cover expansion [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], from reviews of reforestation and afforestation, and from planting with fast-growing, heavy water-using species [ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. The gains are an exclosure-versus-cropland contrast rather than a comparison with unrestored land [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], model projections at regional scale that work through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], a minority of watersheds in a global review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5], and a tentative attribution at sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Some regions in the same model show nonsignificant declines where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. Several units are nulls: the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2], and an FAO–CIFOR review states that interception should put to rest the belief that extensive reforestation or afforestation will increase low flows in the dry season [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. Scale matters within the losses too: the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales in the systematic review [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review finds the runoff reduction significant only in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The lowered water table under new forest is also described as improving drainage, so on waterlogged open land it is not purely a loss [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The review report that China's Grain-for-Green programme, planted mainly with fast-growing non-native species, reduced water supply has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of this roll-up; without that loss inside the restoration families the pool no longer leans negative, so no direction is stated. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: a loss here can coexist with local supply gains reported in the forest restoration water stress row, so read the two side by side rather than netting one against the other. Plantation results are reported in their own family row and do not count here.

justification.mechanism: This row asks how much water leaves the catchment after forest cover is restored or expanded, and the evidence finds both less and more, with close to even weight on each side. Measured syntheses mostly find less: in about 80% of study cases reporting annual water yields the effect of forest restoration and other forms of forest cover expansion was negative, and in 6% positive [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1]; baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]; groundwater levels or recharge decreased with forest cover expansion in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; and no study in the meta-analysis subset showed a water-yield gain [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The reason given is interception and use: tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, and much of the water that soaks in is used by the trees [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed, and that planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]; after clearance, the streamflow gain declines as new cover establishes, and a return to pre-cut totals under natural regrowth may take more than eight years [ev_water_yield_ham08_8]. Planting shows the same: a cited New Zealand study notes afforestation reducing water yield while giving erosion benefits [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4]; a global review warns that large-scale afforestation in water-limited environments will inevitably exacerbate water scarcity [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. On the gain side, baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]; a regional land-climate model projects significant increases of 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% in four regions under full reforestation potential [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]; about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed showed increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% for a 12.6% increase in forest cover [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]; and forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3].
justification.conditionality: What separates the sides is baseline, method, species and time. The losses come from measured syntheses that pool forest restoration with other forms of forest cover expansion [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], from reviews of reforestation and afforestation, and from planting with fast-growing, heavy water-using species [ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. The gains are an exclosure-versus-cropland contrast rather than a comparison with unrestored land [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], model projections at regional scale that work through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], a minority of watersheds in a global review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5], and a tentative attribution at sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Some regions in the same model show nonsignificant declines where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. Several units are nulls: the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2], and an FAO–CIFOR review states that interception should put to rest the belief that extensive reforestation or afforestation will increase low flows in the dry season [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. Scale matters within the losses too: the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales in the systematic review [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review finds the runoff reduction significant only in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The lowered water table under new forest is also described as improving drainage, so on waterlogged open land it is not purely a loss [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The review report that China's Grain-for-Green programme, planted mainly with fast-growing non-native species, reduced water supply has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of this roll-up; without that loss inside the restoration families the pool no longer leans negative, so no direction is stated. Global syntheses agree: more forest cover loss tends to increase annual runoff in both large and small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_1], an increase in forest coverage reduces the share of rainfall leaving as runoff [ev_water_yield_zhou15_1], and changes to forests in water-limited watersheds can lead to larger water-yield responses [ev_water_yield_zhou15_2]. Harvesting or removing forest also raises groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].

effect_mechanism: Keeping forest standing supports children's diets and growth. In a multi-country study of children in rural areas, Rasolofoson et al. find that high exposure to forests causes children to have at least 25% greater dietary diversity than no exposure, an average difference of 0.4 points (95% confidence interval 0.29 to 0.51) against matched non-forest households, and raises the share of households where children ate vitamin A– or iron-rich food by at least 11 and 16 percentage points [ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_1, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_2, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_3, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_4]. A global forest and food-security assessment cites Ickowitz et al. (2014), who found children's dietary diversity rising with community tree cover across 21 African countries, and Johnson et al. (2013), who found that children in Malawi communities that experienced deforestation had less diverse diets [ev_food_security_iufro15_2, ev_food_security_iufro15_1]. Naidoo et al. find that living near multiple-use protected areas with documented tourism would increase children's height-for-age growth scores by 9.8% and reduce the likelihood of stunting by 13.4% [ev_food_security_naidoo19_1]. In India the WOCAT compiler for broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries reports better village self-sufficiency from more and better fodder and more water [ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency].
conditionality: The forest-diet effect depends on community wealth: Rasolofoson et al. find it significant and beneficial in poor communities, insignificant at community GDP between US$3 billion and 5 billion, and reversed above US$5 billion, where forest exposure goes with less diverse children's diets; this is the measured harm on the row [ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_5]. Protected-area gains depend on tourism: no early childhood growth gains were found near protected areas without documented tourism [ev_food_security_naidoo19_2]. Under Mexico's payments for environmental services, as cited in a systematic review, a food index showed a statistically insignificant 0.09 SMD effect [ev_food_security_snilstveit19_1]. Most units compare people living near existing forest or protected areas with people who do not; they show what standing forest provides, not what a protection or community-management project adds, and the tree-cover and deforestation findings are cited second-hand.

conditionality: Restoration can also take agricultural land and reduce on-farm income or employment [ev_household_income_iufro20_7], few studies conclusively show that restored-forest benefits alleviate poverty, which occurs over years or decades when it does [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_4], and Brazil's Reflorestar programme showed no significant effect on municipal GDP, value added or employment [ev_economic_return_seixas24_1]. The same meta-analysis finds no significant effect on income from agricultural sources (SMD = 0.11), on nonagricultural income or on household assets [ev_household_income_snilstveit19_2], so the income gain does not show up as farm income or wealth.

effect_mechanism: Protection and community forest management can reduce poverty through forest income and employment. Community forest management in Nepal reduced both poverty and deforestation in an analysis of 18,000 community forests [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_2], 68% of community forestry cases reporting livelihood outcomes showed income increases (the underlying global review of community forest management counts 316 such cases) [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1], and community forestry in Madagascar had a small but beneficial impact on living standards [ev_household_income_iufro20_2]. Protected areas contributed to poverty alleviation in Costa Rica and Thailand and, in large studies controlling for socio-economic factors, drove poverty reduction [ev_rural_poverty_puri16_1, ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_1]: a meta-analysis of counterfactual studies finds small gains from protected areas in local monetary outcomes (g = 0.028) and poverty outcomes (g = 0.117) [ev_household_income_kandel22_1, ev_rural_poverty_kandel22_1], households in the Chitwan National Park buffer zone of Nepal have 19 percent higher per capita income [ev_household_income_kandel22_2], and across developing countries living within 10 km of protected areas with documented tourism lowers the likelihood of poverty by 16.1%, with poverty 8.8% lower near multiple-use protected areas even without tourism [ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_1, ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_2]. In a systematic review of decentralised forest management, co-management raised regular forest income in Malawi by 26 per cent and by 66% for low-income households, consumption expenditure in Ethiopian participatory forest management communities by 35 per cent, and forest income near Uganda's National Forestry Authority forests by 16 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_1, ev_household_income_samii14_2, ev_household_income_samii14_3, ev_household_income_samii14_6]. World Bank support for participatory forest management raised participating household incomes in Albania by an estimated 30 percent annually and in Honduras by 62 percent, and in Andhra Pradesh, India, poorer households compensated for lost land access gained 40 percent [ev_household_income_ieg13_2, ev_household_income_ieg13_3, ev_household_income_ieg13_4]. In Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla community forestry provides year-round wage labour and a profit share of 10 to 20 thousand pesos per member after harvest [ev_household_income_ceballos21_1], households near GEF forest-management sites in Uganda show income gains [ev_household_income_gefieo19_1], in Bolivia all the main groups selling environmental services improved economically [ev_household_income_robertson05_1], non-timber income rose after benefit-sharing at Bach Ma, Vietnam [ev_household_income_ieg18_3], and WOCAT compilers in India and Afghanistan rate long-term returns as improved [ev_economic_return_wocat_5243_2019_costbenefit_establishment_long, ev_economic_return_wocat_7460_2024_costbenefit_maintenance_long].
conditionality: The pool is divided. The global community-forest review that reports income gains in 68% of cases also records 26% with no change and 6.3% with decreases, and it pools community with household income [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1]. In south-west Madagascar conservation-oriented community management contracts were not profitable and did not raise community incomes [ev_economic_return_ramamo12_1, ev_household_income_ramamo12_1]; the GEF forest-management portfolio has a benefit-cost ratio of 0.69 [ev_economic_return_gefieo19_1]; REDD+ contributions in Nepal were nominal, from 3.2% of the poorest households' income to 0.3% for the less poor, local studies found no effect of REDD+ on material well-being, and an analysis in Indonesia found potentially harmful effects [ev_household_income_iufro20_4, ev_household_income_iufro20_5, ev_household_income_iufro20_6]; payment programmes have a small beneficial or neutral effect on poverty [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_3], and Mexico's payment scheme was less cost-effective than a protected area [ev_economic_return_snilstveit19_2]. Benefits skew to the better-off: in Nepal poor and low-caste households receive much less while bearing more costs [ev_household_income_iufro20_3]; near Uganda's District Forestry Service forests forest income rose by an insignificant 2 per cent and lowest-quartile households lost 6 per cent and 10 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_4, ev_household_income_samii14_5]; at Bach Ma benefits were shared unevenly and two-thirds of product types were over-harvested [ev_household_income_ieg18_3]. Livelihood components often fail: just two out of 37 closed World Bank protected-area projects achieved their livelihood aims, and benefit-sharing around Vietnam's special-use forests averaged US$1,053 per community, too small to have any discernible impact [ev_household_income_ieg13_1, ev_household_income_ieg18_2]. The protected-area studies measure what living near standing forest provides, not the outcome of a restoration intervention; the Colombian benefit of $411–1,236 per hectare a year is a carbon valuation, not cash income [ev_economic_return_wri17_3]; and many figures are secondary citations in reviews or World Bank evaluation estimates without a comparison group. Child diet, stunting and food self-sufficiency findings now sit on the food-insecurity row.

effect_mechanism: In high-income settings tree cover reduces erosion through slope reinforcement and slower runoff: reforestation of just 9.3 percent (159 km2) of New Zealand's Waipaoa catchment could decrease total landslide sediment inputs by about 20 percent [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_6]; afforestation in New Zealand provides erosion reduction benefits [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_3]; reforestation in Slovakia's Hornad watershed is modelled to decrease surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]; and in Taiwan reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2].
conditionality: The New Zealand afforestation benefit comes with reduced water yield [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_3], the Waipaoa and Hornad results are model scenarios [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_6, ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1], and the Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control and check dams, cited in an FAO review [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. A US observation runs the other way on slopes: young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support that its much larger and older predecessors did [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5]. effect_mechanism: Review statements that name restoration generically, not a single family, sit here. An FAO regional review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk, and that natural regeneration and tree planting on failed slopes can help control after-effects such as sediment release into rivers [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1]. An FAO forests-and-water synthesis calls forest restoration one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and lists reducing soil loss and keeping sediment out of streams among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. It cites Taiwan, where reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The effect is off-site for farmers: stabilised slopes and less sediment reaching rivers and reservoirs, at slope and catchment scale rather than on the farm plot.
conditionality: Only the Taiwan unit says how large the effect is, which is why the class is capped; the other statements are FAO assertions without a measured value. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so it cannot be attributed to forest restoration alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The same synthesis is explicit that achieving substantial flood reduction is not among the reasons to rehabilitate watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. The primary landslide and watershed studies behind the Asia review are now registered in their own rows (passive regeneration, active planting and protection). Landslide risk is recorded under erosion here for lack of a landslide category.

An FAO regional review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk, and that natural regeneration and tree planting on failed slopes can help control after-effects such as sediment release into rivers [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1]. An FAO forests-and-water synthesis calls forest restoration one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and lists reducing soil loss and keeping sediment out of streams among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. It cites Taiwan, where reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The effect is off-site for farmers: stabilised slopes and less sediment reaching rivers and reservoirs, at slope and catchment scale rather than on the farm plot.
justification.conditionality: Only the Taiwan unit says how large the effect is, which is why the class is capped; the other statements are FAO assertions without a measured value. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so it cannot be attributed to forest restoration alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The same synthesis is explicit that achieving substantial flood reduction is not among the reasons to rehabilitate watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. The primary landslide and watershed studies behind the Asia review are now registered in their own rows (passive regeneration, active planting and protection). Landslide risk is recorded under erosion here for lack of a landslide category.
